blocks.text: The chapter recalls Israel’s exodus through the image of a loving parent who called a child, taught him to walk, carried him, healed him, and fed him. Israel’s repeated rejection leads toward judgment, but verses 8–9 portray a recoil from total destruction as compassion is kindled. Readers disagree about how this language of divine pathos relates to broader accounts of whether and how God changes.

Matthew’s later use of “out of Egypt I called my son” is a figural rereading of Israel’s exodus in relation to Jesus. It does not remove the verse’s retrospective reference in Hosea to Israel as God’s child.

Hosea has a difficult and varied textual history. The Masoretic text, Old Greek Osee, Qumran witnesses, Targum, Peshitta, and Vulgate sometimes require comparison passage by passage; the Greek translation has distinctive readings but should not be treated as a uniform correction of the Masoretic text. The book also contains northern features alongside later material directed toward Judah, although the evidence does not permit confident assignment of every line to Hosea or to a later editor.

Christian reception of Hosea should remain a later application rather than a replacement of the chapter’s subject. Hosea 11 speaks about Israel, and Christian rereading should not erase Israel, Jewish readers, or continuing Jewish interpretation.
